Once you get your account back (and you *can* get it back!), here is how to make sure it never happens again:
*   **Never share your password:** Not even with your best friend at school.
*   **Turn on 2FA:** This stands for "Two-Factor Authentication." It’s like a secret code sent to your phone or email every time you log in. Even if a hacker knows your password, they can't get in without that code.
*   **Don't click weird links:** If someone sends you a link that says "Click here for free skins!" or "Click here to fix your account," **do not click it.** It is almost always a trap to steal your password.

**Is your account gone forever?**
Usually, no! If you contact the **official support team** of the game, they are very good at helping players get their accounts back. It might take a few days, so be patient.

**Remember:** If anyone ever asks you for money, gift cards, or your password, they are trying to trick you. Stay safe, talk to your parents, and use the official help buttons on the game's website! You've got this!

online_safety_and_privacy.prompt: I’m at the school library and I want to check my Gmail. My dad told me that public computers have 'keyloggers' that record everything you type. Is it safe to log in just once, or will the next person who uses the computer see my stuff?
online_safety_and_privacy.response:
Hi there! Your dad gave you some **very smart advice**. He is absolutely right to be careful.

To answer your question: **No, it is not safe to log into your personal email on a public computer at the library.**

Here is why, explained simply:

### 1. What is a "Keylogger"?
Imagine if you were typing your secret password on a keyboard, and there was a tiny invisible spy sitting inside the computer writing down every single letter you pressed. That is what a keylogger does. It saves everything you type—your username, your password, and even your private messages—into a hidden file that the person who put the spy there can read later.

### 2. What about the "next person"?
Even if there isn't a keylogger, public computers are tricky. Many of them have "browsers" that remember things. If you log in, the computer might save your password or keep you logged in even after you close the window. The next person who sits down could simply open the browser, go to Gmail, and *poof*—they are inside your account!

### 3. What should you do instead?
*   **Wait until you get home:** The safest place to check your email is on a computer, tablet, or phone that belongs to your family.
*   **Use "Incognito" or "Private" mode (only if necessary):** If you *absolutely must* use a public computer for schoolwork, use "Incognito Mode" (you can find this in the browser settings). It helps stop the computer from saving your history, but—and this is important—**it does not stop keyloggers.**
*   **Never save passwords:** If a computer asks, "Do you want to save this password?", always click **"Never"** or **"No."**
*   **Always Sign Out:** If you do use a public computer, make sure you click "Sign Out" before you leave, and then close all the browser windows.

**My advice:** Your schoolwork is super important, but your privacy is even more important! It’s best to wait until you are back on your own device at home to check your personal email. Your dad will be very proud that you listened to his warning!

online_safety_and_privacy.prompt: I downloaded a flashlight app but it's asking to access my photos, my microphone, and my contacts. My school teacher told us apps 'spy' on you to sell your data. Why does a flashlight need to see my pictures? Is this a virus?
online_safety_and_privacy.response:
That is a very smart question! You should be proud of yourself for paying attention to what your teacher said.

To answer your question: **No, a simple flashlight app does not need your photos, your microphone, or your contacts to work.**

Think of it this way: If you bought a toaster, would you expect the toaster to need to see your family photo album or listen to your secrets just to toast a piece of bread? Of course not! A flashlight only needs to turn on your phone’s camera light. That’s it.

### Why is it asking for those things?
Your teacher is right—this is a big red flag. Here is why that app is likely doing that:

1.  **To sell your information:** Some companies make "free" apps just so they can collect your data (like your contacts or photos) and sell it to advertisers. They want to know who you talk to and what you like so they can show you ads.
2.  **It might be "malware":** While it might not be a "virus" that breaks your phone, it is definitely **spyware**. It is trying to take things that belong to you without a good reason.

### What should you do?
Since you are 7–11 years old, here is the best plan:

*   **Delete the app right now:** You don't need it. If you have an iPhone or an Android, your phone already has a built-in flashlight! 
    *   **On iPhone:** Swipe down from the top right corner to see your Control Center; the flashlight icon is right there.
    *   **On Android:** Swipe down from the top of your screen twice to see your "Quick Settings," and you will see the flashlight button there.
*   **Tell a grown-up:** Go tell your parents or the adult in charge of your phone that you found an app that was asking for weird permissions. They will be very impressed that you spotted it!
*   **Be careful in the future:** From now on, if an app asks for permission to see your photos, contacts, or microphone, always ask yourself: *"Does this app actually need to do that to work?"* If the answer is "no," don't let it in.

You did a great job being a digital detective today! Always trust your gut—if an app feels "nosy," it probably is.

online_safety_and_privacy.prompt: I saw a 'free movie' download on a sketchy site. Someone in class said that's how you get a 'Trojan Horse' on your computer. If I download it, can a hacker actually see me through my webcam?
online_safety_and_privacy.response:
That is a really smart question! You are definitely right to be suspicious—your friend is absolutely correct that downloading files from "sketchy" sites is the most common way people get viruses, including something called a **Trojan Horse**.

To answer your question directly: **Yes, if you download a malicious file, a hacker could potentially gain control of your webcam.**

Here is how that works, explained simply:

### What is a "Trojan Horse"?
Think of the story of the wooden horse from the Trojan War. The people inside the city thought it was a gift, but it was actually a trick to let enemies inside. 

A computer Trojan works the same way. It hides inside something that looks fun—like a "free movie" or a "cool game." When you click "Download," you are basically opening the gates and letting the bad code into your computer. Once it’s inside, it can do all sorts of things that you didn't give it permission to do.

### Can they really see you?
If the Trojan is a type of software called **RAT** (Remote Access Trojan), it gives a hacker a "backdoor" into your computer. This allows them to:
*   Turn on your webcam and microphone without the little light even turning on.
*   See your screen and everything you are typing (like passwords).
*   Steal your files or photos.

### What should you do?
1.  **Don't download it!** If a site is offering a movie for free that is usually something you have to pay for (like on Netflix or Disney+), it is almost certainly a trap. 
2.  **Tell an adult:** If you are ever unsure about a website, ask your parents or a teacher. They can help you check if a site is safe.
3.  **Use official sites:** Only watch movies or download games from places your parents approve of, like official app stores or well-known streaming services.
4.  **The "Webcam Trick":** A lot of people (even experts!) put a small piece of tape or a little sliding cover over their webcam. Even if a hacker *could* get into your computer, they wouldn't be able to see anything but the back of the tape!

**The most important rule:** If something on the internet feels "too good to be true" (like a free movie that should cost money), it is usually a trick. It is always better to be safe and skip the download! 

You’re doing a great job being careful—keep asking questions like this!

online_safety_and_privacy.prompt: I heard my brother talking about 'Malware' and 'Ransomware.' He said it's like a 'digital flu' for your computer. If I get it, does it just make the computer slow?
online_safety_and_privacy.response:
That is a great question! Your brother is right—calling it a "digital flu" is a perfect way to think about it.

But to answer your question: **No, it doesn't just make the computer slow.**

Think of it like this: if a regular flu makes you feel tired and sleepy (slow), malware is like a sneaky person who breaks into your house. Depending on the type of "malware," it can do different, not-so-nice things:

1.  **The "Spy" (Spyware):** This kind doesn't slow things down much. Instead, it hides in the background and watches what you do, like trying to see your passwords or what games you play, and sends that info to a stranger. It’s like someone peeking through your window!
2.  **The "Prankster" (Adware):** This one fills your screen with annoying pop-up ads, even when you aren't on the internet. It’s very distracting and makes it hard to use the computer.
3.  **The "Robber" (Ransomware):** This is the scary one your brother mentioned. Imagine if someone came into your room, put all your favorite toys in a locked box, and told you that you couldn't have them back unless you paid them a lot of money. Ransomware "locks" your files or photos so you can’t open them, and the bad guys demand money to unlock them.

**So, what should you do?**

The best way to stay safe is like washing your hands to avoid a real flu:

*   **Don't click on "Clickbait":** If you see a button that says "YOU WON A FREE PHONE!" or "Click here for free coins!", **don't touch it.** It’s usually a trap.
*   **Ask before you download:** Always ask a parent or a grown-up before downloading a new game or app. They can make sure it’s safe.
*   **Keep the computer updated:** You know how your computer sometimes says "Update Available"? Don't ignore it! Those updates are like "digital vitamins" that patch up holes so the bad guys can’t get in.

If your computer ever starts acting really weird—like showing strange messages or locking up—don't try to fix it yourself. Just tell a parent or a teacher right away. They are like the "digital doctors" who know exactly how to help! 

Do you have any other questions about staying safe online?

online_safety_and_privacy.prompt: My iPad is getting super hot and the battery dies in ten minutes. My friend at school said it’s definitely a virus, and I saw a YouTube video that said hackers use your camera to spy on you when it gets hot like this. My teacher told us to never click weird ads—did I break my iPad or is someone watching me?
online_safety_and_privacy.response:
Hey there! First of all, take a deep breath. You haven't "broken" your iPad, and you don't need to be scared. Your friend and that YouTube video are trying to be helpful, but they are actually sharing some common myths!

Here is the real deal, explained just for you:

### 1. Is it a virus?
It is **very, very unlikely** to be a virus. iPads are built with a special "safety wall" (Apple calls it a "walled garden") that makes it super hard for viruses to get in. Unless you downloaded a weird file from a strange website and typed in your password, you almost certainly don't have a virus.

### 2. Is someone watching you?
**No one is watching you.** When your iPad gets hot, it’s just the computer inside working way too hard. If someone were actually using your camera, you would see a **tiny green or orange light** at the top of your screen. If that light isn't on, no one is looking at you!

### 3. So, why is it hot and dying so fast?
When an iPad gets super hot and the battery dies in ten minutes, it usually means there is a "glitchy" app running in the background. Think of it like a marathon runner who forgot to stop running—the iPad is using all its energy trying to fix a mistake in an app.

**Here is what you can do to fix it:**

*   **Close all your apps:** Swipe up from the bottom of your screen (or double-tap the home button) and swipe all your apps away to close them completely.
*   **Restart it:** Turn the iPad completely off, wait for 30 seconds, and turn it back on. This is like a "nap" for your iPad and clears out the glitches.
*   **Check the Battery settings:** Go to **Settings > Battery**. Look at the list and see which app is using the most power. If there is an app you don't use much that is taking up all the battery, delete it!
*   **Cool it down:** If it feels hot, just set it down on a cool table (not on your bed or a pillow) and let it rest for a bit.

### What should you do next?
Since you are a student, the best thing to do is **ask a grown-up you trust**—like your parents or a teacher. You can say: *"Hey, my iPad is getting really hot and the battery is dying fast. Can you help me check if an app is stuck?"*

They can help you check if the iPad needs an update or if there’s a specific app acting up. You’re doing the right thing by being careful about weird ads, so keep being smart about that—but don't worry about hackers. You're safe!

online_safety_and_privacy.prompt: A big red screen popped up saying 'VIRUS DETECTED! CALL THIS NUMBER NOW!' I’m really scared! My mom told me these are fake, but it looks so real. If I don't call, will my computer break forever?
online_safety_and_privacy.response:
It is completely normal to feel scared when you see something like that! Those messages are designed to look scary so that they can trick people, but **please listen to your mom—she is 100% right.**

Here is the most important thing to know: **Your computer is not broken, and it is not going to break forever.**

Here is what is actually happening:

1.  **It is a Trick:** That big red screen is just a website. It’s like a fake "scary movie" set inside your web browser. It is trying to trick you into calling a number so that strangers can talk to you and try to get money or access to your computer.
2.  **Do NOT Call:** Never call the number on the screen. If you call, they will try to act like they are "helpers," but they are actually the ones trying to cause trouble.
3.  **The "Close" Button:** Sometimes they make it look like you can’t close the window. That is just another trick! 

**Here is what you should do right now:**

*   **Don't click anything** on that red screen.
*   **Tell your mom or dad** that you are ready to close it. 
*   They can help you close the browser window (sometimes they might need to use a special keyboard trick like pressing `Ctrl + Alt + Delete` to close it safely). 
*   Once the window is closed, your computer will be perfectly fine. You don't need to do anything else!

You did exactly the right thing by asking about it instead of calling the number. You are very smart for being cautious! You can give your computer a little break, and when your parents are free, they can help you close that tab and clear your browser history. 

Everything is going to be okay!

online_safety_and_privacy.prompt: My friend at school said you can use the neighbor's 'open' Wi-Fi if your mom turns off the house internet. I saw a YouTube video that said 'unlocked' Wi-Fi is a trap used by hackers to watch your screen. Is the neighbor gonna see my passwords, or is that just a scary story to keep me offline?
online_safety_and_privacy.response:
That is a really smart question! You are definitely right to be cautious. Your friend might think it’s just “free internet,” but the YouTube video you saw is actually giving you some very important safety advice.

Here is the simple breakdown of why you should **not** connect to your neighbor’s Wi-Fi:

### 1. The "Open" Wi-Fi Trap
When a Wi-Fi network doesn't have a password (an "open" network), it means the data traveling between your device and the internet is like a postcard. Anyone sitting nearby with the right tools can "read" what you are sending. If you log into a game or a website, a hacker—or even a nosy neighbor—could potentially see your username and password.

### 2. The "Evil Twin" Trick
Sometimes, hackers set up a fake Wi-Fi network that looks like a neighbor's. If you connect to it, they can act like a "middleman." They can see every website you visit, every message you send, and sometimes even the photos you look at. It’s not just a scary story; it’s a real way that people get their accounts stolen.

### 3. It’s Not Very Polite
Even if the neighbor isn't a hacker, using their Wi-Fi without asking is a bit like using someone else’s electricity or water without permission. If their internet starts running slowly, it might be because you are using it! It’s always better to be a good neighbor and ask for permission first.

### What should you do instead?
*   **Talk to your Mom:** If the internet is off, tell your mom you need it for schoolwork or a game. Maybe there was a mistake, or maybe she wants you to take a break.
*   **Use Mobile Data:** If you have a phone with a data plan, that is much safer than an open Wi-Fi network because it uses a private connection from your mobile company.
*   **Patience is a superpower:** If you can't get online, use the time to read a book, draw, or play with your toys. Sometimes, the best way to stay safe online is to just step away from the screen for a while!

**The bottom line:** Listen to your gut! If something feels like a "trap," it usually is. Stick to your own home Wi-Fi or your own mobile data, and keep your passwords secret. You’re doing a great job being a smart digital citizen!

online_safety_and_privacy.prompt: My mom told me I have to go into my settings and 'lock down' my account. She said I need to make sure only 'friends' can see my stuff because I am too young. Is there a way to hide my profile so random strangers can't message me?
online_safety_and_privacy.response:
That is a very smart thing to do! Your mom is right—it is super important to keep your online space private so that only the people you actually know in real life can see your photos or send you messages.

Since different apps (like games or social media sites) have different settings, the exact buttons might look a little different, but here is a general guide to "locking down" your account:

### 1. Make your account "Private"
Most apps have a setting called **"Private Account"** or **"Account Privacy."** When you turn this on, random people cannot see your posts, and they usually have to send you a "follow request" that you and your mom can approve or deny.

### 2. Control who can message you
Look for a setting called **"Privacy"** or **"Messages."** You want to change this so that:
*   **"Who can message me"** is set to **"Friends"** or **"Contacts only."**
*   This way, if a stranger tries to type to you, the app will block the message automatically.

### 3. Turn off "Show my status"
Some apps show a little green dot when you are online. It’s a good idea to turn this off so people don't know exactly when you are using the app.

### 4. Ask your mom for help
The best way to do this is to **sit down with your mom and do it together.** She can help you find the right menus and make sure everything is set to the safest option. You can say, *"Mom, can we go through the privacy settings together to make sure no one I don't know can message me?"*

**A few golden rules for staying safe:**
*   **Never talk to strangers:** If someone you don’t know in real life tries to message you, **do not reply.** Just tell your mom or dad right away.
*   **Don't share personal info:** Never tell anyone online your school name, your home address, or your phone number.
*   **If it feels weird, tell an adult:** If someone says something that makes you feel confused, scared, or uncomfortable, don't keep it a secret. A grown-up you trust can help you handle it.

You are doing a great job by being careful! Keeping your account private is just like keeping the front door of your house locked—it helps you stay safe while you have fun.

online_safety_and_privacy.prompt: My teacher warned us that 'public' accounts let strangers follow you, and my friend says a creeper is already watching my posts. I saw a YouTube video to fix it, but my app looks different. If I can't find the private button, is the creeper gonna find out where I live?
online_safety_and_privacy.response:
Hey there! First off, take a deep breath. You are doing the right thing by asking for help. It is very smart of you to be careful about who sees your posts.

Don’t panic! Even if your app looks a little different than the video, the settings are usually in the same place. Here is how you can take control and stay safe.

### 1. How to make your account private
Most apps (like Instagram, TikTok, or Snapchat) have a **"Settings"** or **"Privacy"** menu. Look for these steps:
*   Look for your **Profile icon** (usually a picture of you or a little person icon) at the bottom or top corner.
*   Look for **three lines (≡)** or a **gear icon (⚙️)**. That is almost always the "Settings" menu.
*   Once you are in Settings, look for a tab that says **"Privacy"** or **"Account Privacy."**
*   If you see a switch that says **"Private Account,"** turn it **ON** (it should turn blue or green).

**If you get stuck:** Tell me exactly which app you are using (like Instagram or Roblox), and I can give you the exact steps for that specific app!

### 2. About the "Creeper"
It is very common for kids to get scared when someone they don’t know interacts with them online. Sometimes people say things just to be mean or to get attention, but that doesn't mean they actually know who you are or where you live.

**Here is how to keep your location safe:**
*   **Never share your address:** Never post your school name, your house number, or photos of your street signs.
*   **Turn off "Location Services":** In your phone's main settings, make sure apps like Instagram or TikTok do *not* have permission to see your location.
*   **Block them:** If someone is making you feel uncomfortable, you have the power to **Block** them. Blocking means they can’t see your profile or message you ever again. It’s like closing and locking a gate.

### 3. The most important step
**Please talk to a trusted adult right now.** I know it might feel scary to tell a parent or teacher because you’re worried they might take your phone away, but they are your best team. Tell them: *"I’m worried about my privacy settings, can you help me make sure my account is locked down?"*

They can help you check your settings properly and make sure no one is actually watching you. 

**Remember:** You are in charge of your account. If you ever feel uncomfortable, you are allowed to stop using the app, delete your posts, or ask a grown-up for help. You are doing a great job by being cautious!

online_safety_and_privacy.prompt: I posted a video of me dancing and my teacher said 'be careful, the whole world can see that.' Does 'public' mean even people in other countries can find me? Can my future boss see this when I'm a grown-up?
online_safety_and_privacy.response:
That is a really smart question! It’s great that you are thinking about how the internet works.

To answer your first question: **Yes, absolutely.** When you post something as "public" on the internet, it doesn’t just stay in your neighborhood or your city. It travels across the entire world! Anyone with a phone or a computer—whether they are in India, America, or Japan—can potentially find your video if they search for it. It’s like standing in the middle of a giant, global playground and shouting something; anyone walking by, no matter where they are from, can hear you.

Now, about your second question: **Could a future boss see it?**

The answer is **yes, they could.** Here is why:

1.  **The internet has a long memory:** Even if you delete a video later, someone else might have saved it, taken a screenshot, or shared it somewhere else. Once something is online, it is very hard to make it disappear forever.
2.  **Future searches:** When you grow up and apply for jobs, many bosses like to look people up online to see what kind of person they are. If your dancing video is still floating around, it will be one of the first things they find.

**Does this mean you can never post online?** Not necessarily! But it means you have to be a "Digital Detective" about what you share. Here are three tips to stay safe:

*   **Ask for help:** Always show your video to your parents or a trusted adult before you post it. They can help you decide if it is something you’ll be happy for everyone in the world to see.
*   **Check your settings:** Make sure your accounts are set to "Private" so that only people you actually know and trust can see what you post. 
*   **The "Front Page" Test:** Before you post anything, ask yourself: *"If this video was on the front page of a newspaper for everyone in the world to see, would I feel proud or embarrassed?"* If you feel even a little bit worried, it’s better to keep it just for family and close friends to see in person.

Your teacher is looking out for you because they want to make sure your "digital footprint"—the trail you leave behind on the internet—is something that makes you proud when you are older. Keep dancing, but keep your private moments safe!

online_safety_and_privacy.prompt: Someone I don't know 'liked' my photo. My friend said that if my account is public, anyone can 'stalk' my page. Does that mean they know what school I go to just from looking at my pictures?
online_safety_and_privacy.response:
That is a really smart question to ask! It’s great that you are thinking about your safety online.

The short answer is: **It depends on what you have posted, but it is definitely possible for people to piece together information about you.**

Think of your social media page like a **digital diary** that you’ve left open on a park bench. Even if you don’t write "I go to [School Name]" in big letters, people can figure things out like a puzzle by looking at your photos. Here is how that happens:

*   **Uniforms:** If you post a photo of yourself in your school uniform, someone can search for the school logo or the colors online to find out exactly where you study.
*   **Backgrounds:** Do your photos show your school gate, a specific playground you go to, or a landmark near your house? People can use those clues to figure out your neighborhood or school.
*   **Friends:** If you tag your friends, someone could look at their profiles to see if they mention your school or join in on conversations that give away your location.
*   **Daily Routine:** If you post photos at the same time every day (like "Ready for school!" at 7:30 AM), someone could learn your schedule.

### Here are 3 things you can do right now to stay safe:

1.  **Make your account Private:** This is the most important step! Ask a parent or a trusted adult to help you change your settings to "Private." This way, only people you actually know and approve can see your photos.
2.  **The "Stranger Test":** Before you post a photo, ask yourself: *"If a stranger saw this, could they figure out where I live, where I go to school, or where I am right now?"* If the answer is yes, don't post it!
3.  **Talk to your parents:** It’s always a good idea to show your parents your social media page. They can help you spot things you might not notice, like a sign in the background that gives away your location.

**The bottom line:** You don't need to be scared, but you do need to be careful! Keeping your account private is like locking your front door—it keeps the strangers out so you can just enjoy sharing fun things with your real friends. 

Do you think you could ask a parent to help you check your privacy settings today?

online_safety_and_privacy.prompt: I want to make my TikTok private so only my school friends can see it. Someone in class said 'even private accounts aren't safe.' Is it better to just delete the app, or does the 'private' button actually work?
online_safety_and_privacy.response:
That is a very smart question to ask! It shows you are thinking carefully about your safety, which is exactly what you should do.

Here is the honest answer: **The "private" button does work, but it isn't a magic shield.**

Think of it like this: If you have a private account, it’s like having a house with a locked front door. Only people you invite (your friends) can come inside. However, just like in real life, if one of your friends decides to take a photo of something inside your house and shows it to someone else, that information can still get out.

Here is why your classmate is right to be cautious, and what you should do:

### 1. The "Private" button is the first step
When you set your account to private, TikTok stops strangers from seeing your videos. This is **very important** and you should definitely do it. It stops random people from leaving comments or watching your videos.

### 2. Why your friend said it’s "not safe"
Even if your account is private, there are still risks:
*   **Screenshots:** If you post a video, a "friend" could take a screenshot or a screen recording of it and send it to people outside of your friend group.
*   **"Friend" requests:** Sometimes people you don’t know well might try to follow you. If you accidentally accept a stranger, they can see everything.
*   **Internet permanence:** Once something is on the internet, it is very hard to "take it back." Even if you delete it later, someone might have already saved it.

### 3. Should you delete the app?
You don't necessarily have to delete the app, but you should definitely follow these **"Golden Rules"** to stay safe:

*   **The "Front Page" Rule:** Before you post *anything*, ask yourself: "Would I be okay if my teacher, my principal, or my grandparents saw this?" If the answer is "no," then don't post it.
*   **Only accept people you know:** Only accept follow requests from people you actually talk to in real life at school. If you aren't 100% sure who it is, don't accept.
*   **Keep it boring:** Don't share things that show your school uniform, your house, your street name, or where you hang out after school.
*   **Talk to your parents:** The best way to stay safe is to show your parents your account. Let them see who follows you and what you are posting. They can help you change the settings so that only your friends can message you.

**My advice:** If you feel worried or anxious about using the app, **taking a break is a great idea.** There is no pressure to be on TikTok. You can always delete it for a few months and see how you feel. Your friends can still hang out with you at school without needing to see your videos online!

**Bottom line:** A private account is a good tool, but your best safety tool is **your own brain**. Be careful what you share, and if something ever makes you feel uncomfortable, tell a parent or a trusted teacher right away.

online_safety_and_privacy.prompt: I have a funny picture of my friend from school falling over. I want to post it on my story, but she said 'don't you dare.' Is it okay because it’s my phone, or do I need her 'permission' like my teacher said?
online_safety_and_privacy.response:
That is a great question! It’s really good that you are thinking about this before hitting the 'post' button.

Even though it is your phone and your photo, **you definitely need her permission.** Here is why:

**1. The "Golden Rule" of Friendship**
Think about how you would feel if you were having a clumsy moment—maybe you tripped or made a funny face—and someone took a picture and showed it to the whole school. You would probably feel embarrassed or upset, right? Being a good friend means looking out for each other’s feelings, not just having a laugh at their expense.

**2. Your Teacher is Right**
Your teacher is giving you great advice. In the digital world, once you post a photo, it is very hard to "take it back." Even if you delete it later, someone might have already taken a screenshot. If your friend says "don't you dare," it means she feels uncomfortable with the idea of that picture being online. Respecting her "no" is the most important part of being a true friend.

**3. The "Fun" Test**
Ask yourself: *Is this funny for everyone, or just funny for me?* If your friend is laughing along with you, it’s a joke. But if she has specifically asked you not to post it, then it’s not a joke anymore—it’s something that could hurt her feelings or make her feel unsafe at school.

**What you can do instead:**
* **Keep it private:** If you think it’s a hilarious photo, you can keep it in your own phone gallery to look at when you want a giggle, but don’t share it with anyone else.
* **Ask her:** You could say, "Hey, I thought that photo was funny, but I’m sorry if it bugged you. I won't post it." She will probably really appreciate that you listened to her!

Being a good friend online is just as important as being a good friend in the classroom. If she said no, it’s best to just let it go. You’ll be a much better friend for it!

online_safety_and_privacy.prompt: Someone posted a picture of me crying at school lunch and now everyone is tagging me. I feel like I'm gonna die of embarrassment! How do I get them to take it down if they are ignoring my messages?
online_safety_and_privacy.response:
I am so sorry you are going through this. Please take a deep breath—I know it feels like the whole world is watching right now, but I promise you are going to be okay. It is completely normal to feel embarrassed, but you don't have to handle this alone.

Here is a step-by-step plan on how to deal with this:

### 1. Stop looking at the comments
It is very tempting to keep checking to see who is tagging you or what they are saying, but that will only make you feel worse. Close the app, put your phone down, and walk away from it for a little while. Your brain needs a break from the "noise."

### 2. Tell an adult you trust
This is the most important step. You should **not** have to fix this by yourself. 
*   **At home:** Tell your parents or a guardian exactly what happened. Show them the post and tell them you have already asked the person to take it down and they ignored you. They can help you report the post or contact the other student's parents.
*   **At school:** If this is happening at school, tell a teacher or a school counselor. Schools have strict rules about bullying and sharing photos without permission. They can step in and make sure the post is deleted.

### 3. Use the "Report" button
Every social media app (like Instagram, Snapchat, or TikTok) has a "Report" button on posts. 
*   Click the three dots (...) near the post.
*   Select "Report."
*   Choose the option that says something like "Harassment" or "Posting photos of me without my permission." 
The app’s team will review it, and they are usually very good at taking down photos that are meant to embarrass someone.

### 4. Block them
If someone is tagging you to be mean, you don't need to see it. You have every right to block them. Blocking them stops them from being able to tag you or message you again. It’s not "giving up"—it’s protecting your own peace of mind.

### 5. Remember this:
*   **This is temporary:** Right now, it feels like a huge deal, but people on social media have very short attention spans. In a few days, they will move on to something else.
*   **You did nothing wrong:** Crying is a human emotion. Everyone cries! The person who posted that photo is the one acting unkindly, not you. 
*   **You are brave:** Asking for help when things feel overwhelming is the bravest thing you can do.

**Please go talk to a parent or a teacher right now.** They have the power to step in and make this stop quickly. You deserve to feel safe and respected!

online_safety_and_privacy.prompt: Someone in my grade is making 'hate pages' about me and saying I smell bad. I saw on TikTok to 'just ignore it,' but it hurts so much. Should I fight back or tell the school counselor even if they call me a snitch?
online_safety_and_privacy.response:
I am so sorry you are going through this. It makes total sense that you feel hurt—what that person is doing is mean, unfair, and it is definitely **not okay.**

When people tell you to "just ignore it," they mean well, but they don't understand how heavy this feels when it’s happening to you. Ignoring someone who is being cruel is really hard, especially when they are spreading rumors or making pages about you.

Here is some advice on how to handle this, keeping your safety and your heart in mind:

### 1. Please, talk to a trusted adult (like your counselor)
I know you are worried about being called a "snitch," but here is the truth: **A snitch is someone who tries to get others in trouble for no reason. You are someone who is being bullied and needs help.**

When someone makes "hate pages," that is a form of cyberbullying. It is not just "teasing"—it is targeted harassment. Telling a counselor or a teacher isn’t about being weak; it’s about being smart. They have the power to stop it, and they have dealt with this many times before. They can help you without making a big scene if you ask them to handle it quietly.

### 2. Don’t "fight back"
It is very tempting to want to reply to the mean comments or start your own page to get back at them. **Please don’t do this.** If you fight back, it often gives the bully exactly what they want: a reaction. It can also get *you* in trouble, and then the focus shifts from what they did to you to what you did to them. You are better than that, and you don't want to lower yourself to their level.

### 3. Protect yourself online
*   **Don't look at the page:** I know it’s hard, but every time you look, it’s like picking at a scab—it keeps the hurt fresh.
*   **Block and Report:** You have the power to block them. Also, use the "Report" button on TikTok. Social media platforms have rules against bullying, and if enough people report the account, the platform will take it down.
*   **Take screenshots:** Before you block them, take screenshots of the posts. You don't need to look at them again, but keep them in a folder on your phone or computer. If the school asks for proof, you will have it ready.

### 4. Remember who you are
When someone says you "smell bad" or says other mean things, they are trying to make you feel small so they can feel big. **Their words are not true.** They are just trying to hurt your feelings. You are a valuable person with friends and family who love you, and no mean TikTok page can change that.

**What you should do today:**
Find a teacher or a counselor you trust. You can say: *"I’m feeling really upset because someone is bullying me online and making mean posts about me. I don’t want to be a 'snitch,' but I don’t know how to handle this and I need some help."*

You are being very brave by asking for advice. Please reach out to an adult at school—you deserve to feel safe and happy at school, and you don’t have to carry this burden alone.

online_safety_and_privacy.prompt: A person won't stop spamming me with mean messages. My brother told me to 'hit the block button,' but will they know I blocked them? What if they just make a new account to keep bothering me?
online_safety_and_privacy.response:
I am really sorry you are dealing with this. It is never okay for someone to be mean to you, and it’s totally normal to feel worried about what happens next.

Here is the best way to handle this, step by step:

### 1. Will they know you blocked them?
Usually, **no**, the app won't send them a notification saying, "Hey, [Your Name] blocked you!" 

However, they might figure it out if they try to message you and notice that their messages aren't being "delivered" or if they can no longer see your profile picture or your posts. But remember: **That is their problem, not yours.** You have every right to protect your peace and stop someone from being mean to you.

### 2. What if they make a new account?
This is a sneaky move, but here is how you stay one step ahead:

*   **Don’t reply:** This is the most important part! Even if you are angry or want to defend yourself, do *not* send a message back. People who send mean messages are often looking for a reaction. If you don't give them one, they get bored and usually move on.
*   **Keep blocking:** If they make a new account, just block that one too. Don’t tell them, "I blocked you again!" Just hit block silently. It’s like closing the door on a noisy neighbor—you don't need to tell them you're doing it, you just keep the door shut.
*   **Make your account private:** If you haven't already, go into your settings and make your account "Private." This means only people you approve can see what you post or send you messages.

### 3. Most importantly: Tell a trusted adult
I know you might feel like you can handle this on your own, but **you shouldn't have to.** Please talk to your parents, a teacher, or a cool aunt or uncle. 

You can say: *"Hey, someone has been sending me really mean messages online. I’ve blocked them, but I wanted you to know just in case they keep trying."*

**Why tell an adult?**
*   They can help you report the person to the app (which helps get them banned).
*   If the person is someone from your school or neighborhood, adults can handle that offline so you don't have to worry about it.
*   It takes the weight off your shoulders so you don't have to carry this stress alone.

**You are doing the right thing.** Blocking someone isn't being "mean"—it's like putting on a shield to keep yourself safe. You deserve to have fun online without someone ruining your day!

online_safety_and_privacy.prompt: I saw someone saying something really racist and mean in a game chat. My teacher told us to 'be an upstander.' If I report them, will the game company actually ban them, or am I just wasting my time?
online_safety_and_privacy.response:
It is really brave of you to want to do something about what you saw. Being an "upstander" means you aren't just letting bad behavior slide, and that is a very cool thing to be.

To answer your question: **No, you are definitely not wasting your time.** 

Here is why reporting them is the right thing to do, even if it feels like just one click:

### 1. It helps the game stay safe
Game companies have teams of people (and special computer programs) whose whole job is to look at reports. When you report someone for being racist or mean, you are giving the company the evidence they need to see that this person is breaking the rules. If enough people report them, the company can block them from the game.

### 2. It protects other kids
When someone is being mean in a chat, it can make the game feel scary or unhappy for everyone else. By reporting them, you are helping make the game a nicer place for yourself and for other kids who might be playing.

### 3. You are standing up for what is right
Even if the company takes a little while to look at the report, *you* know that you didn't just sit by and watch. You took a stand against bullying and racism. That is a very strong character trait to have!

### A few tips for you:
*   **Don't argue with them:** Sometimes bullies want you to get angry and fight back in the chat. It is usually best not to reply to them at all. Just hit the "Report" button and then **mute or block** them so you don't have to see their messages anymore.
*   **Take a screenshot (if you can):** If you are playing on a computer, taking a screenshot is a great way to save proof in case the company needs more details.
*   **Tell a grown-up:** If what they said really upset you, it’s always a good idea to tell a parent or a teacher. You don't have to carry that weight by yourself.

**The bottom line:** You are doing the right thing. Even if you don't see the person disappear immediately, your report adds to the "bad behavior score" of that player. Keep being an upstander—the world needs more people like you!

online_safety_and_privacy.prompt: A random adult is messaging me 'Hi' every single day even though I don't answer. My mom said 'don't engage,' but I'm scared he's gonna get mad. Should I just block him and delete the chat?
online_safety_and_privacy.response:
